title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Skin, Hair & Nail Assessment—Pressure Injury Risk and Early Change
html:
An integumentary assessment examines skin color, temperature, moisture, texture, turgor, integrity, sensation, lesions, hair, scalp, and nails. The RN looks for local change, systemic illness, impaired perfusion, infection, pressure or device injury, moisture damage, and altered healing. Accurate assessment depends on comparison with the client’s usual skin tone and nearby tissue—not on a single color word.

Learning goals

  • Collect a focused history of skin, hair, nail, wound, and pressure-injury concerns.
  • Inspect the skin systematically, including pressure points, folds, perineum, scalp, and device contact areas.
  • Assess color change across skin tones using visual and palpation findings.
  • Describe lesions and skin breakdown objectively without assigning an unsupported diagnosis.
  • Recognize pressure, moisture, perfusion, allergic, infectious, and systemic warning patterns.
  • Document location, measurements, interventions, communication, and reassessment.

Begin with stability and urgent patterns

Observe overall color, temperature impression, moisture, breathing, circulation, and mental status before beginning a routine skin examination. A new widespread rash with facial or tongue swelling, wheezing, stridor, hypotension, or difficulty breathing requires immediate airway and emergency response. Rapidly spreading redness or discoloration with severe pain, fever, hypotension, crepitus, or toxicity; blistering or peeling with mucosal involvement; widespread petechiae with systemic illness; or cool, clammy, cyanotic skin with altered mental status also requires urgent escalation.

Color is only one pressure-injury cue
On deeply pigmented skin, early pressure damage may not appear bright red and blanching can be difficult to see. Compare with surrounding tissue and assess localized warmth or coolness, firmness or softness, pain, edema, and persistent darker, purple, or other discoloration.

Ask a focused integumentary history

Ask about pain, itching, burning, numbness, dryness, sweating, rash, bruising, color change, wounds, drainage, swelling, hair loss, scalp symptoms, and nail changes. Clarify onset, location, spread, triggers, exposures, new soaps or products, foods, travel, insect contacts, illness, fever, and what has been tried. Ask whether a lesion has changed in size, shape, border, color, surface, bleeding, or healing.

Review skin conditions, pressure injuries, vascular disease, diabetes, neuropathy, allergies, immune compromise, incontinence, mobility and repositioning ability, nutrition and hydration, recent surgery, radiation, adhesives, dressings, and medical devices. Review medications that affect bleeding, immune response, photosensitivity, moisture, or healing. Ask about sun exposure and protection without assuming risk from skin tone alone.

Inspect systematically and protect dignity

Explain the assessment, obtain consent before touch, ensure warm surroundings and adequate light, and expose one region at a time. Use gloves when contact with nonintact skin, mucosa, drainage, or body fluids is anticipated. Follow transmission precautions for a potentially contagious condition. Compare both sides and adjacent tissue.

Inspect from head to toe rather than only where the client reports symptoms. Include scalp and hair, behind ears, under breasts and abdominal folds, axillae, elbows, sacrum and coccyx, hips, ischia, perineum, heels, ankles, between digits, and beneath removable devices during routine care when safe. Oxygen tubing, masks, cervical collars, splints, casts, compression devices, catheters, and other equipment can create pressure, friction, shear, or moisture.

Assess color across skin tones

Compare current color with the client’s usual appearance and surrounding areas. Pallor, cyanosis, jaundice, erythema, bruising, and mottling may appear differently with pigmentation, lighting, perfusion, and temperature. Inspect more than one site. Oral mucosa, lips, conjunctivae, palms, soles, and nail beds can add information, but no site or color alone establishes oxygenation, perfusion, anemia, or liver dysfunction.

Palpate a discolored area for temperature, firmness, edema, moisture, and tenderness. Ask the client what is new. Document the color actually seen—such as darker brown, violaceous, dusky, pale, or yellow—rather than using “redness” for every skin tone. Correlate with vital signs, respiratory effort, pulse quality, capillary refill, laboratory data, medications, and systemic symptoms.

Palpate temperature, moisture, texture, turgor, and edema

Use the backs of the hands to compare temperature and finger pads to assess texture, tenderness, firmness, moisture, and edema. Local warmth may accompany inflammation or infection; a cool extremity may reflect reduced perfusion. Diaphoresis can occur with fever, pain, hypoglycemia, shock, medication effects, or other conditions. Interpret the whole cue cluster.

Skin turgor is only one hydration clue and becomes less reliable with aging and reduced elasticity. Choose an appropriate site and combine the result with mucous membranes, thirst, weight trend, intake and output, urine concentration, vital signs, perfusion, and laboratory findings. Describe edema by location, laterality, extent, pitting or nonpitting method, and skin condition using the organization’s scale.

Describe lesions before naming them

Use a consistent structure: exact anatomic location and side; number; distribution; size in centimeters; shape; color; border; elevation or depth; surface; surrounding skin; warmth; tenderness; drainage and odor after cleansing as appropriate; and change over time. Terms such as macule, papule, vesicle, pustule, plaque, nodule, wheal, scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, or fissure describe morphology when used correctly. They do not establish the underlying disease.

For a pigmented lesion, note asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter, and evolution when present and arrange appropriate evaluation. Do not reassure solely because a lesion is small or painless. Photograph only with consent and according to organizational policy, using approved secure systems and measurement standards.

Identify early pressure-related change

Pressure injury can occur over a bony prominence or beneath a medical device because of pressure combined with shear. Inspect high-risk areas and ask about localized pain before visible breakdown appears. Test blanching gently when appropriate, but recognize that visual blanching may be difficult to evaluate in darkly pigmented skin.

An intact localized area of nonblanchable erythema may meet criteria for a Stage 1 pressure injury. In darker skin, persistent discoloration, warmth or coolness, firmness or softness, pain, or edema may be the more visible early cues. Relieve pressure immediately, reassess, protect from friction and moisture, and implement the individualized prevention plan. Do not massage a discolored bony prominence.

Stage 2 describes partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis or a qualifying serum-filled blister; it is not used for moisture-associated skin damage, adhesive injury, skin tears, or burns. Stage 3 and 4 involve full-thickness loss at different depths. If slough or eschar obscures the extent of tissue loss, the injury is unstageable until enough of the wound bed is visible. Deep tissue pressure injury has persistent deep red, maroon, purple discoloration or blood-filled blister and may evolve despite treatment. Follow the current staging policy and consult wound expertise when findings are uncertain.

Risk tools support—but never replace—inspection

Use the organization’s validated pressure-injury risk tool at required times and after condition change. Evaluate sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction and shear, perfusion, devices, and other client-specific risks. A score does not authorize skipping a skin assessment, and a low-risk score does not make a new discolored area normal.

Match prevention to the risk pattern: individualized repositioning and pressure redistribution; heel offloading; moisture and incontinence care; nutrition and hydration support; safe movement that reduces shear; device fit and skin checks; and client education. Document whether interventions were actually implemented and evaluate the skin response.

Assess hair, scalp, and nails

Inspect hair distribution, texture, breakage, and localized or diffuse loss. Separate the hair to view the scalp for lesions, scale, wounds, infestation, tenderness, and drainage when indicated. Use gloves and appropriate precautions when infestation or contagious disease is suspected.

Inspect nails for color, contour, thickness, splitting, lesions, surrounding inflammation, and clubbing. Nail changes can reflect local trauma, infection, circulation, chronic illness, grooming, or normal variation. Capillary refill contributes to perfusion assessment but should be interpreted with temperature, pulse, color, and systemic findings.

Respect delegation boundaries

Assistive personnel may observe skin during hygiene, repositioning, toileting, and device care and report changes according to training and policy. The RN validates new discoloration, pain, warmth, breakdown, rash, bruising, or drainage; performs the focused assessment; determines urgency and staging within policy; implements and evaluates the plan; and communicates concerns. “The aide applied barrier cream” does not close the assessment loop.

Document findings another clinician can locate

Record assessment time and position; usual and current color; temperature, moisture, texture and turgor; precise lesion or wound location; size and depth using approved method; shape, border, surface and surrounding skin; blanching response when assessed; pain; drainage; device relationship; pressure-risk score and factors; interventions; communication; and reassessment. Avoid “skin good,” “rash present,” or copied staging without current evidence.

For example: “0730: Right heel intact with 2.0 × 1.5 cm persistent violaceous area, warmer and firmer than adjacent tissue; does not visibly blanch; client reports new tenderness 4/10. Heel offloaded and repositioning plan initiated; wound-resource RN notified 0740. Reassessment scheduled per protocol.” This describes the finding without relying on bright redness.

Clinical example

During morning hygiene, an assistive team member reports a “dark spot” beneath a client’s oxygen mask. The RN removes and reapplies the device safely, assesses breathing first, then compares the affected bridge of the nose with nearby skin. The area is darker, warmer, firm, and tender but intact. The RN relieves pressure with the approved device strategy, documents measurements and device relationship, notifies the appropriate team, and reassesses rather than dismissing the finding because it is not red.
